title: Berkshire 2005 letter: float, moats, the Gotrocks, and CEO option math
summary: Buffett's 2005 letter covers insurance float, why acquisitions for stock cost shareholders, widening the moat over short-term earnings, and the cost of derivatives and delay. It also exposes how fixed-price options reward CEOs for retained earnings and explains how Wall Street "Helpers" shrink investor returns.

principles.text: Float is wonderful only if it doesn't come at a high price; its cost is set by underwriting results.
principles.quote: Float is wonderful – if it doesn’t come at a high price. Its cost is determined by underwriting results, meaning how the expenses and losses we will ultimately pay compare with the premiums we have received.

principles.text: Issuing stock for acquisitions means the acquirer's owners sell part of everything they own.
principles.quote: When a management proudly acquires another company for stock, the shareholders of the acquirer are concurrently selling part of their interest in everything they own.

principles.text: Widen the moat: when short-term and long-term conflict, long-term competitive position takes precedence.
principles.quote: We always, of course, hope to earn more money in the short-term. But when short-term and long-term conflict, widening the moat must take precedence.

principles.text: Act immediately on problems in personnel or operations; delay is costly.
principles.quote: When a problem exists, whether in personnel or in business operations, the time to act is now.

principles.text: Owners in aggregate can only earn what their businesses earn; frictional costs of Helpers reduce returns.
principles.quote: For investors as a whole, returns decrease as motion increases.

principles.text: Avoid significant debt: a string of great numbers multiplied by a single zero is zero.
principles.quote: a long string of impressive numbers multiplied by a single zero always equals zero.
